name: Rimless glasses

card.summary: Rimless glasses mount the lenses directly to the bridge and temples with no frame around them, so the eyewear covers less of the face.
card.note: Lenses are more exposed to damage; polycarbonate is the lens material labs commonly require.

quick.overview:
Rimless glasses have lenses held by screws or small bushings attached to a bridge and temples, with no rim around the lens. Because there is little visible frame, they are described as inconspicuous and are chosen by people who want to wear glasses without the frame dominating the face.

For appearance, the draw is that eyes, brows and the upper face stay visible. Forum members describe them as a good option for people who dislike how glasses look, and they have been associated with lightweight titanium frames. No clinical research has examined how frame style affects attractiveness in this specific case.
quick.how: Wearers pick a lens shape (round, oval, octagon and others) and a mount type: screw mounts or bushing mounts, with three-piece designs allowing adjustable nose pads. Frames are typically paired with lightweight materials such as titanium and polycarbonate lenses. An optician mounts the lenses and adjusts the fit.
quick.risks: Without a frame, lenses take more stress and labs report three-piece frames need lens replacement more often than other designs. Some labs only mount polycarbonate lenses in rimless frames because CR-39 lacks impact resistance. Bushing mounts are harder for non-professionals to repair.

lead: Rimless glasses attach the lenses directly to a bridge and temple arms, using small screws or hollow plastic double rivets known as bushings, so no frame surrounds the lens.[1] They are described as inconspicuous, and the style has never fully gone out of fashion.[1]

For people who want to wear glasses but keep attention on the face, this is the appeal: with almost no visible frame, the eyes, brow line and cheek area stay uncovered. Forum members on T Nation describe being 'a fan of the smaller rimless designs' because they dislike how glasses look, and others praise the look as sophisticated.[2][3]

Wikipedia traces the design to the 1880s, when it emerged partly to reduce the weight of heavy glass lenses in metal frames. The style was popular into the 1960s, revived in the 1980s and rose again in the 2000s with light titanium frames.[1]

chain: Lenses are mounted with no surrounding frame
Less frame material covers the eyes, brows and cheeks
Glasses look lighter and the face reads as more open
angle.text: Rimless glasses reduce the visual footprint of corrective eyewear. Wearers who find standard frames obstructive or dominant use them to keep their face visible while still wearing a prescription.

infobox: Lenses attached with screws or bushings to bridge and temples

paras: Lenses are mounted either with small screws or with bushings, hollow plastic rivets fitted into holes in the lens, which lock onto barbed metal pins on the bridge and temples.[1] There are two main types: three-piece glasses, with a bridge and two separate temples, and rimways (also called cortlands), which add an arch linking the temples to the bridge for added stability.[1]
Lens shapes have included circles, ovals, octagons and panto shapes. Round lenses became an icon after Steve Jobs wore them, and demand rose after his death in 2011, according to Wikipedia.[1]

A rimless monocle appeared in the 1820s and the modern design emerged in the 1880s. Early versions were mostly pince-nez, popularised in the early 1900s partly by Theodore Roosevelt's public image. Three-piece styles with nose pads arrived around 1920 and overtook pince-nez, and rimways appeared in the 1920s.[1]

Advantages described by Wikipedia include light weight, especially with titanium and polycarbonate; no frame material obstructing vision; and a less conspicuous look. Three-piece designs with nose pads allow adjustments to fit.[1]

Drawbacks include greater susceptibility to damage. Labs report three-piece frames need new lenses two to ten times more often than other designs, CR-39 lenses lack impact resistance, and some labs process only polycarbonate for rimless frames.[1]

On T Nation, members mention rimless glasses in passing: one praises a poster's rimless glasses as 'sexy', and another says he prefers the smaller rimless designs because he dislikes wearing glasses, adding that they suit an 'intellectual' look.[2][3] These are individual taste comments rather than studies.

timeline.event: Three-piece styles with nose pads arrive.[1]
Rimless frames rise again with lightweight titanium.[1]
